newsitem.title: USA: PRESS DIGEST - New York Times business - April 29.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - New York Times business - April 29.

text.p: The New York Times reported the following business stories on Tuesday:
* The Dow Jones industrials ended up 44.15 points at 6,783.02, helped by a rally in blue-chip shares.
* Marvel Entertainment announced a proposed reorganization plan that would involve a merger with Toy Biz, while bondholders, led by Carl Icahn, said they intended to oppose the plan.
* Fast-food restaurant operator CKE Restaurants said it would buy troubled hamburger chain Hardee's from Imasco for about $327 million.
* Boeing shares fell as it reported first quarter earnings that were higher compared to a year ago but results which were short of expectations.
* Paxson Communications is in negotiations to purchase New York City TV station WBIS, owned by Dow Jones and ITT for about $250 million, according to a person familiar with the talks.
* March new single-family home sales declined 2.5 percent, after rising in February.
* Mexican businessman Carlos Peralta Quintero, a partner with Bell Atlantic in a cellular phone company, was acquitted of tax fraud charges.
* Metro-Goldwyn Mayer agreed to buy Metromedia's film and television units for $573 million.
* Boeing and other large companies with much money at stake are already lobbying Congress on renewing China's normal trading status.
* While Britain's statistics point to a strong economy, they obscure the poorer sides of the country.
* EchoStar Communications DISH.O said News Corp indicated it might pull out of a $1 billion satellite-television venture.
* The growing bond between industry and academia has raised questions about the reliability of information on drugs and other medical therapies.
* Manhattan's Fifth Avenue was ranked the world's most expensive retail strip for the third year in a row.
* Engineers at Daimler-Benz are developing a Mercedes that gives access to the Internet.
* Advertising: Coca-Cola's new "Coca-Cola Incredible Summer" advertising campaign, involving debit cards and Coke merchandise, seems to challenge PepsiCo's "Pepsi Stuff" campaign.
* Louis Simpson, the man who might replace Warren Buffett at Berkshire Hathaway should he retire, is private and low-key, but, like Buffett, an iconclastic investor.
